cim: Artificial Intelligence and the Engels’ Pause
cim_eredeti: Artificial Intelligence and the Engels’ Pause
szoveg_eredeti:
Over the past two years we have heard many exciting predictions about the benefits of Artificial Intelligence with people like Elon Musk predicting that AI and robotics will drive an era of “incredible abundance”; we are told that there will be nothing AI cannot do better than people except perhaps “being human”. Other AI experts such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei point to ambitious 10-year hopes for tackling major diseases like cancer and in the most recent UK budget, our Labour government has promised a major package of investment to unlock the opportunities of AI.

Occasionally, AI experts admit to the danger of systems ‘going rogue’ but a less dramatic, but more likely problem is largely dismissed.

On the BBC this morning (15th Nov) there was a segment about the introduction of AI in N. Ireland and the fear of AI taking our jobs was briefly raised. However, we were reminded that when calculators were introduced this did not result in accountants becoming unemployed and we were reassured that during the Industrial Revolution the new technology brought economic growth and wealth rather than unemployment.

Let’s look at some of the claims about new technology bringing wealth.

The Industrial Revolution in the UK lasted roughly from 1760 to 1830, and if you remember your GCSE history you will recall the development of steam engines, which led to mechanised weaving, and then to factories, trains, steamships, and the modern economy. When I studied history at school we were taught about the successes of the Industrial Revolution but little attention was paid to the downsides.

Before the Industrial Revolution, weaving was a skilled ‘cottage industry’, usually performed in the homes of the weavers who could work to their own schedule from home and make a reasonable living. When those skilled home weavers found themselves being undercut by steam-powered factory looms that could do their work faster and for a much lower price, some of them facing unemployment and poverty, tried to stand in the way of industrial progress by joining gangs who vandalised steam-powered looms and factories. These gangs were called Luddites. They were violently suppressed with 17 Luddites hanged and several hundred transported to the colonies. Our history teacher was not unsympathetic but we were told the word ‘Luddite’ became an insult for someone standing in the way of progress.

Historical scholarship has developed and improved since I was at school; in 2009, a New York professor called Robert Allen introduced the concept of the ‘Engels’ Pause’ to explain what happened during the British Industrial Revolution. Professor Allen points out that while GDP per person increased by 46% in the period between 1780 and 1840, the average wage only increased by 12% across this 60-year period. During the first 60 years of the Industrial Revolution the economy grew rapidly and factory owners gained immense wealth, but living and working conditions for ordinary labourers generally worsened before they eventually improved many decades later. Professor Allen described this long gap between GDP growth and wage growth as the ‘Engels’ Pause’ in honour of Friedrich Engels who wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England, where he argues that the Industrial Revolution had made workers worse off. He argued that the industrial workers had lower incomes than their pre-industrial peers and they lived in more unhealthy and unpleasant environments. He shows, for example, that in large industrial cities mortality from disease was four times that in the surrounding countryside, and mortality from convulsions was ten times as high.

For two generations of workers (30 years each) there was enormous disruption in the UK, with people moving from the countryside into cities, working gruelling 12-to-14-hour shifts with hazardous machinery and strict workplace discipline, but with very little increase in their pay. The fact that later generations gained economically, especially after Trade Unions organised better pay and conditions, will have been little comfort to the workers who lived through the first 60 years of the Industrial Revolution.

The impact of information technology on work has been a feature during much of my life. I am a retired teacher and spent my last 25 years of work as Head of ICT Department at a large secondary school where I was known as an evangelist for new technology, so I am not instinctively opposed to the use of AI.

However, as someone who was responsible for the purchase of new ICT equipment, I have enough sense to be sceptical about the promises made by IT salesmen. They have a job to do, they want to sell their technology and make a profit, any claims they make should be treated with caution. They are not the enemy, but nor are they your friends.

During the 1980s and ’90s the impact of ICT on employment patterns was significant with factory employment in the UK dropping from 6.8 million in 1980 to 4.1 million in 2000. Some of this was due to foreign competition, but automation was a major factor. A University of Sheffield study claims UK manufacturing output actually grew during the 1980s and 1990s, even as millions of factory jobs disappeared. This confirms that technological efficiency, rather than just factory closures, was replacing manual labour.

In TV journalism, ICT had a major effect with widespread job losses as film crews switched from film to videotape. The new technology allowed instant playback, allowing 24-hour news schedules and continuous pressure on journalists.

The introduction of electronic layout of newspapers (desktop publishing) led to massive job losses among compositors. In January 1986, Rupert Murdoch secretly moved production of several newspapers from Fleet Street to a high-tech plant in Wapping, East London, where just 670 workers replaced 6,800 traditional print roles, displacing roughly 90% of the printing workforce.

In all of these cases, the long-term profitability of the companies improved, but many of those who lost their jobs suffered poverty as a result, even if future generations benefited from the new technology.

In the first industrial revolution there was a long ‘Engels Pause’ while business owners grew very rich before the workforce started to benefit. The question must be asked, will the AI revolution have a similar pause, with most of the profit going to the owners of large businesses, while ordinary people suffer unemployment and poverty, just as the first generation suffered in the Industrial Revolution.

In June this year, Elon Musk became the world’s first trillionaire – he is worth more than the annual GDP of smaller countries such as Poland, Switzerland or Sweden. New technologies allow those at the top to grow very rich, but those working for billionaires often do not prosper. Musk’s first actions when he took over Twitter involved firing many of the staff. The second richest person in the world is Jeff Bezos, but his staff at Amazon do not always prosper. Amazon centre workers are tracked by automated systems that monitor “time off task” and enforce strict pick-and-pack rates, which can reach hundreds of items per hour. There are allegations that Amazon staff are discouraged from joining trade unions.

The clear lessons from history are that:

Individual tasks disappear faster than entire jobs. Workers who are restricted to a single narrow task are most likely to lose out to AI.

Resisting new technology tends to fail. Just as the Luddites could not stop steam-powered factories, we cannot stop businesses adopting AI, but what we have to do is to ensure that workers retain some control over how AI is introduced and who benefits.
